title: Beating the Bell Curve
author: Matthew Evans
summary: A former headteacher unpacks the recurring 'forgotten third' debate over GCSE grades 1-3, arguing that GCSE outcomes are essentially a bell curve driven mostly by general cognitive ability, conscientiousness, and environment. He evaluates three strategies — beating, masking, or side-stepping the bell curve — and concludes the answer isn't new vocational qualifications but better teaching of core subjects, a broader range of GCSEs that reward domain-specific aptitude, and changing the stigmatizing language around low grades.
points: The 'forgotten third' debate resurfaces cyclically because a system that makes a third of students feel like failures after 11 years of schooling satisfies no one.
GCSE performance breaks down roughly into general cognitive ability (~50%), conscientiousness/environment, and specific domain aptitude (~20%), varying by subject.
A 2017 Cambridge Assessment report found 68% of students' grades cluster within one grade of their average, showing the bell curve's grip.
Vocational qualifications aren't the fix: GCSEs already reward students who can dance, build, cook, program, and create — the real problem is stigmatizing language around grades 1-3.
Proposed fixes: teach low attainers better in core subjects, expand aptitude-rewarding GCSE options, rebrand low grades as a 'Level 1 Pass,' and ease Progress 8 rules.
quotes: Of all the educational Groundhog Days, the ‘forgotten third’ rhetoric feels like the hardest doom-loop to escape.
It is for this reason that GCSE outcomes fall into the classic bell-curve shape.

We should also keep trying to beat the bell-curve, particularly in core subjects.
